report:
Your “no” is too absolute. For **nonpregnant women with recurrent uncomplicated cystitis/UTI**, the best current evidence says cranberry products **probably give a modest preventive benefit**, not a reliable one. The 2023 Cochrane review found cranberry products probably reduce symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs: RR 0.74 (95% CI 0.55–0.99), moderate-certainty evidence; benefit was not shown for elderly institutionalized people, neurogenic bladder/incomplete emptying, or pregnancy. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10108827/

Guidelines reflect this nuance: AUA/CUA/SUFU say clinicians **should offer cranberry as an option** for women with recurrent UTIs (moderate recommendation, grade B in the update), while emphasizing proven measures such as vaginal estrogen for peri/post-menopausal women and antibiotic strategies when appropriate. https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/recurrent-uti NICE is more antibiotic-focused and treats self-care evidence as limited/secondary. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng112/chapter/recommendations

Trials are inconsistent: an early BMJ trial of cranberry-lingonberry concentrate reduced recurrence, https://www.bmj.com/content/322/7302/1571 but later juice trials were negative, likely due to dose, adherence, sugar load, and variable proanthocyanidin content. Practical conclusion: don’t rely on cranberry alone or use it to treat infection; if trying prevention, prefer standardized extract/capsules with stated PAC dose for several months, and reassess.
